title: Current aggregate income, price, labor, and household-room signals move on different clocks
source_unit: Deliberately non-pooled BEA aggregate accounts, BLS consumer/producer prices and labor surveys, and Federal Reserve SHED household responses

observations.period: July 2026; BEA personal income and outlays

denominator.unit: aggregate US personal-income and outlays accounts; flows and rates, not household respondents

personal_income_change.unit: billions of current US dollars from June; 0.4% monthly rate

disposable_income_change.unit: billions of current US dollars from June; 0.5% monthly rate

pce_change.unit: billions of current US dollars from June; 0.2% monthly rate

services_minus_goods_change.unit: billions of current US dollars; arithmetic contrast of reported changes

observations.method: BEA monthly national income and product accounts release; current-dollar flows and personal saving rate are retained without converting them into household-level welfare.
observations.uncertainty: Aggregate current-dollar flows can reflect prices, composition, transfers, tax timing, revisions, and spending timing; services/goods changes are not a stated preference or cultural shift.
observations.subgroup: National aggregates only; no household, worker, income, or place subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: Income and consumption can rise while selected households lose liquidity or face higher costs; a 3.0% aggregate saving rate is not a direct resilience measure.

denominator.unit: CPI-U US city-average index built from BLS price quotations and expenditure weights; release does not disclose a single respondent denominator

all_items_monthly.unit: percent seasonally adjusted change from July

observations.method: BLS CPI-U August 2026 release; seasonally adjusted monthly and unadjusted twelve-month rates are kept distinct.
observations.uncertainty: CPI-U is an aggregate urban price index, not a household-specific basket or affordability measure; exposure varies by vehicle use, housing, contracts, location, and ability to substitute.
observations.subgroup: US city-average index categories; no household or income subgroup in this observation.
observations.counterinterpretation: A high energy rate does not mean every household bore the same increase or reduced consumption; monthly index movement does not establish political attribution.

observations.period: August 2026; PPI final and intermediate demand

denominator.unit: BLS producer-price index sample and weighting system; release does not disclose a single respondent or transaction-count denominator

diesel_monthly.unit: percent monthly increase in detailed final-demand goods index

observations.method: BLS August 2026 PPI release preserving final-demand, detailed energy, and intermediate-demand indexes.
observations.uncertainty: Producer-price movement can be absorbed by margins, contracts, inventories, substitution, or productivity, or passed through later; it does not establish consumer incidence, firm market power, or household burden.
observations.subgroup: Producer and intermediate-demand index categories; no firm-size or household-exposure subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: A sharp diesel movement can affect transport, agriculture, logistics, and prices differently depending on fuel intensity, contracts, routes, and bargaining position.

denominator.unit: thousands of civilian labor-force participants age 16+ in CPS; establishment payroll denominator is separate and not disclosed in this extraction

payroll_change.unit: thousands of nonfarm payroll jobs from July; August preliminary

long_term_unemployment_share.unit: percent of unemployed people unemployed 27 weeks or more

observations.method: BLS CPS household and CES establishment surveys kept separate; August establishment estimate is preliminary where marked.
observations.uncertainty: Payroll jobs are not unique workers and nominal average earnings are not real purchasing power, job quality, schedule control, or household security. CPS and CES have different universes.
observations.subgroup: Civilian population/labor force in CPS and total nonfarm establishments in CES; selected industries have separate change measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Positive payroll growth and 4.1% unemployment can coexist with involuntary part-time work, long-term unemployment, unequal access, weak bargaining power, or rising costs.

denominator.unit: available monthly seasonally adjusted total-nonfarm JOLTS rate observations; July preliminary

openings_rate.unit: percent arithmetic mean of January-July monthly rate

observations.method: Arithmetic mean of seven BLS seasonally adjusted monthly JOLTS total-nonfarm rates from public series pages.
observations.uncertainty: Partial-year values may be revised and July is preliminary; establishment rates summarize employer reports, not unique workers, motivations, job quality, or household welfare.
observations.subgroup: Total nonfarm establishments; no worker demographic, occupation, or AI-exposure subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low quits can reflect reduced outside options, preference, retirement, sector composition, or measurement limits; this is not an AI displacement estimate.

observations.period: 2025; SHED household hardship and price-response context

denominator.unit: published percentage base among adults or within family-income groups; questions have different reference periods

food_insufficiency.unit: percent reporting household food insufficiency in prior month

low_high_income_food_gap.unit: percent food insufficiency among family income under $25,000 versus $100,000+

observations.method: Federal Reserve SHED 2025 published estimates; prior-month food and bill measures are kept separate from price-change comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: Rounded population estimates with different reference periods; this is not a same-respondent price-to-food causal sequence or a direct comparison to aggregate CPI.
observations.subgroup: All adults and family-income groups; income and hardship fields have source-specific universes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Household hardship can remain high while aggregate income grows; the survey does not identify the precise price, benefit, job, or health event behind each response.

related_sources.claim: BEA July 2026 personal income and outlays release.
BLS CPI program and August 2026 release context.
BLS PPI program and August 2026 release context.
BLS Employment Situation release and CPS/CES definitions.
Federal Reserve SHED household hardship source.

boundary: This is a current-vintage macro-to-household comparison. It does not establish that CPI/PPI movements caused a household outcome, that income or payroll growth restored household room, or that the aggregate labor market changed trust, politics, culture, or geopolitical behavior. A same-household or same-worker dated event with exposure, adaptation, attribution, and recovery remains open.
